blueprint_topic: Management of Care — multidisciplinary tumor-board review and patient-centered cancer treatment planning
stem: A client with a newly diagnosed, complex cancer asks why the case will be presented at a multidisciplinary tumor board. Which explanation by the RN is most accurate?

options.A: Specialists from different disciplines review the clinical information and treatment options together to develop a coordinated plan that informs discussion with the client.
options.B: The board confirms the treatment proposed by the primary oncology specialty and focuses mainly on coordinating procedure dates across participating departments.
options.C: The board makes the treatment decision in place of the treating team so the client receives a finalized plan after the multidisciplinary review is complete.
options.D: The board concentrates on pathology and imaging interpretation, while each oncology specialty develops its treatment recommendations separately afterward.

rationale: A is correct. The National Cancer Institute defines tumor board review as a treatment-planning process in which cancer physicians and other healthcare specialists meet regularly to review and discuss new or complex cancer cases, with the goal of deciding as a group on the best treatment plan for a patient. NCI defines multidisciplinary care as treatment planning involving professionals from different specialties and defines shared decision-making as a process in which the patient and healthcare professional work together, considering the patient's values, goals, and concerns. Therefore, tumor-board review supports coordinated multidisciplinary treatment planning that informs subsequent patient-centered discussion. B is incorrect because tumor-board review is not primarily an administrative scheduling meeting or a mechanism merely to confirm one specialty's plan. C is incorrect because multidisciplinary review does not eliminate the treating team's and patient's roles in treatment discussion and decision-making. D is incorrect because the board's purpose includes discussion of treatment planning across disciplines rather than limiting the meeting to pathology/imaging while treatment recommendations remain siloed.
educational_objective: Explain tumor-board review as coordinated multidisciplinary clinical treatment planning for new or complex cancer cases that informs patient-centered discussion rather than replacing the treating team's and client's decision-making roles.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: NCI Dictionary of Cancer Terms — tumor board review; multidisciplinary; shared decision making
source_version_date: Current NCI Dictionary resources rechecked 2026-08-20; NCI Dictionary terms are maintained and reviewed in the current web resource
source_locator: NCI Dictionary — 'tumor board review': a treatment-planning process in which a group of cancer doctors and other healthcare specialists regularly review/discuss new and complex cancer cases, with the goal of deciding as a group on the best treatment plan; potential participants include medical/radiation oncologists, surgeons, pathologists, radiologists, genetics experts, nurses, physical therapists, and social workers. NCI Dictionary — 'multidisciplinary': a treatment-planning approach/team with experts from different specialties. NCI Dictionary — 'shared decision making': patient and healthcare professional work together to decide the best plan while considering patient values, goals, concerns, options, risks, and benefits.
source_claim_supported: Current NCI guidance directly supports tumor-board review as multidisciplinary clinical treatment planning for new or complex cancer cases and supports preserving patient-centered shared decision-making rather than treating the board as an administrative meeting or substitute for patient/team discussion.

pdf_visual_verification: The NCI evidence relied upon for this item is current HTML; no NCI PDF is relied upon. Relevant NCSBN 2026 Management of Care collaboration/client-rights content had been visually verified earlier in this audit session.
targeted_near_duplicate_check: Repository-targeted search for 'tumor board multidisciplinary cancer treatment planning specialists review complex case patient decision' returned no indexed matching files; no near-duplicate identified by the targeted check.
correction_summary: Retained the tumor-board construct but removed the 'only one specialty' absolute and longest-key cue. The revised distractors test realistic misconceptions involving administrative confirmation of one specialty's plan, transferring decision authority away from the treating team/client, and fragmenting diagnostic review from multidisciplinary treatment planning.

option_audit.A: Correct; directly reflects NCI's multidisciplinary tumor-board treatment-planning definition while preserving patient-centered discussion.
option_audit.B: Plausible administrative/confirmation misconception; incorrect because tumor-board review is clinical multidisciplinary treatment planning rather than mainly scheduling or validating one specialty's plan.
option_audit.C: Plausible authority-transfer misconception; incorrect because tumor-board review does not eliminate the treating team's or patient's role in treatment decisions.
option_audit.D: Plausible diagnostic-only misconception; incorrect because tumor boards review and discuss treatment options across disciplines rather than leaving treatment recommendations siloed after the meeting.

cueing_audit.absolute_words: No option relies on always/never/only/all/must-type absolutes.
cueing_audit.answer_length: All four alternatives contain comparable multidisciplinary-planning detail; the key is not uniquely signaled by length.
cueing_audit.grammatical_lexical: All four alternatives are parallel explanations of the purpose and authority of the tumor board.
cueing_audit.second_answer_risk: No defensible second answer identified after current NCI source-based audit and targeted repository search.
